utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Udo for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, Professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. Unfortunately, Mr. Zdravko Mucic is absent today, because he is talking to his investigator from Bosnia in the detention unit and he has not waived his right for the hearing to continue in his absence. At the same time, I wish to inform the court that colleague Michael Greaves, at the request of Mr. Mucic, has gone to the detention unit for further consultations with the investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, before you sit down, what do you mean by he has not waived his rights to be present? What do you mean by that? Nobody made it uncomfortable for him to be here. He was here, quietly, and everybody allowed him what ever rights he could exercise. He on his own stayed away -- I do not know what he thought he was doing by that. Nobody interfered with him exercising a right not to be here, if he so wishes. Now you are telling the Trial Chamber that he has not waived his rights. What do we do when he does not come -- that the Trial Chamber should wait for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand your concern, and it is clear to me that the trial has to respect certain rules. It is also clear that his Defence counsel has to be present in the courtroom, but all I am able to do is to convey the instructions of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They are instructions you should keep to yourself and not make yourself look like an extraordinary thing by relating it to anybody. Telling this to anybody makes you look something awkward -- telling the Trial Chamber how your client voluntarily stayed away and telling the Trial Chamber that he had not waived his right to be present. What was he doing when he was staying away? The Trial Chamber takes it that he has waived his right to be present and we accept that waiver as sufficient for the Trial Chamber to continue until he thinks, or by your own wisdom you could make him see reason to attend. Perhaps he has not understood that the Prosecution has closed its case and it is his duty to make his Defence. Until the gravity of what he is doing is appreciated, you know what to tell him. Let us have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Cynthia McMurrey and, along with Ms. Nancy Boler from the United States, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the witness so that Ms.. Residovic will continue her examination-in-chief? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed SEFKIJA KEVRIC (continued)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Kevric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest after a very tiring day yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Kevric, explaining your role with respect to the supply of food for the army, the refugees and detained persons, you said that this was the most difficult period of your life. Mr. Kevric, could you please tell us what did you dispose of in -- what did you have at your disposal in your logistic department to be able to prepare food for all these persons, as you have been explaining to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The logistic agency at the time was responsible for the supply and preparation of food for all the units of the TO, of the MUP, for a certain number of refugees, the prison, and for the Igman enterprise. We lacked the most essential food products to be able to prepare normal meals. We did not have any meat, fresh vegetables, potatoes, carrots, onions and spices. As the responsible person who was quite versed in these matters, I can say that, with the articles that we had at our disposal, such as noodles, soup and rice, we were not able to prepare food better than we did. The food that we did prepare could not even be delivered to the units, or, rather, to the end users, because we lacked the containers for transporting it. We had five or six thermos containers of 25 to 30 litres capacity each, which were faulty, they could not close properly, so that, in the course of transportation to the end users, the food would lose 25 to 30 per cent in quality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kevric. Tell me, please, may I ask you now what was the situation with respect to flour and bread; did you, at the time, that is, in the spring and summer of 1992, have sufficient quantities of flour to be able to make bread?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did have certain quantities of flour, but they were nowhere near sufficient, in view of the large number of people who depended on us for their meals, not to mention the rest of the population and the enormous number of refugees who were in Konjic at the time, or were passing through Konjic to go on to Jablanica in the direction of Croatia. We had to reduce the minimum standard when manufacturing bread, which meant, also, reducing the quantity of bread per person when distributing the bread among the end users. I already said yesterday that we received the first quantity of flour in the middle of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, can you tell me whether there were any problems with the preparation of bread, that is, in view of the constant threat of war and the repeated shelling, did you have problems in baking the bread?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were problems with the baking process, because the municipal bakery of Konjic was in the same direction as the post office and the railway station and other buildings, which were of significance for the Konjic municipality, so that the artillery targeting from Borci hit the bakery on a number of occasions. It was hit five or six times so that, in those periods, we were unable to produce bread, nor could the bakery function. To provide the minimum amount of bread, we obtained it from the Jablanica municipality, but these were such small quantities. There were about 13,000 refugees in Jablanica, the population, the army, the MUP and the HVO, so that the quantity we received, we sought to distribute first among the hospital and the wounded and the people on the front-lines of defence. I myself, as the assistant commander for logistics, and my staff, would often be left without bread.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, the food, such as it was and that was prepared within your department, was it the same in quality and quantity regardless of the users, or were there any differences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The food was prepared in the same place according to the number of registered users, with the help of lists or by phone, if there was no possibility of delivering those lists, and then these forms were checked, the food was prepared on the basis of standards which were reduced significantly and upon the completion of the preparation of food, all the users were given the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified yesterday that, as part of your duties, you visited the Celebici barracks several times, or, rather, the underground depot for the purpose of control and distribution of weapons held there. Mr. Kevric, my question is: during these visits of yours, did you meet any one of the detainees and perhaps did you talk to any one of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When touring or visiting the people working in the Celebici warehouse, I talked to Mr. -- actually he was a prisoner at the time -- my colleague from secondary school, Slavko Saran. On that occasion, Slavko Saran did not tell me anything regarding the conditions in the prison, nor did he mention any kind of mistreatment. We simply spoke about our lives since we had graduated from secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, did you, at any point in time in 1992, apart from always going along the upper path to the warehouse, did you ever enter the buildings in which the prisoners were detained? Before that, may I ask you whether you know -- whether you could show us on this model where the prisoners were detained -- in which of these hangars. If you know, will you please point it out to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I will show it to you. (Witness indicates with pointer on model).

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, whether at any point in time in 1992 you were close to this building, or actually entered the building where the detainees were held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I say at the very outset that I had visited this area before as well, because the road leading to our warehouse is 20 to 30 metres away. However, I cannot recall exactly -- it was in the summer -- whether it was in August or September, I really could not say -- a commission of the OECD came to the TO staff, which was then housed in the 3rd of March elementary school. They were received by the commander and, after talking to the commander, Enver Tahirovic and myself were asked by the commander to take the commission to the Celebici prison. Upon arrival at the Celebici prison, I entered the prison for the first time. The prisoners all got up when we entered, the delegation consisted of four or five people. Heading the delegation was, I think, a dark skinned gentleman -- whether he was American or English, I really do not know -- and they started talking to the prisoners in our presence. The gentleman who headed the delegation asked us whether we would agree to go out so that they could talk to the prisoners. We agreed and we left. They talked to the prisoners. When they came out, they did not tell us anything about their conversations with the prisoners, but, as far as I was able to judge, they were satisfied and they thanked us. After that, I stayed in the Celebici warehouse and Mr. Enver Tahirovic took the members of the commission to the Musala prison. What happened at Musala, I really do not know. That is as much as I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, as you have just told us that that was the first time you entered the building in which the prisoners were detained, tell us whether you noticed on any one of these persons detained there any kind of injuries, any evidence of disease, any visible traces that would distinguish them from other people that you came across in the same period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will tell you truthfully the way it was. First of all, I had never been in a prison, so when I entered the prison, we stopped at the very entrance to the prison so that we did not really have time to look around. Perhaps if we had been present throughout that conversation, I could tell you more. I was really unable to see anything in the short period while we entered, because after a minute or two we left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, who actually gave you the order to take this delegation to the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received an oral order from my commander, Mr. Esad Ramic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, did this delegation ask you or Mr. Enver Tahirovic in your presence any questions with regard to the management and the running of the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this commission indeed did not ask us any questions. We simply went in our vehicle and the commission went in their own vehicle. We came to the prison, we entered it, and that was it. I really cannot say anything else about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, did you arrive in front of this structure at that time, or did you engage in conversation with some other person -- some third persons on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this time, I really cannot remember and say whether anybody from the administration of the camp, or I should say the prison, was present with us. That, I cannot speak to -- I cannot say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you personally or somebody from your staff -- did you ever receive any written report on the visit of this delegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never found out, as a member of the staff, anything about the visit of this delegation, and I believe that we would have been told something about it, because we were accompanying this delegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago, you said that your school friend, Saran, did not complain to you about any abuse are regard to himself or any of his colleagues. Now, let me ask you something else. First, in general, you explained how the food was prepared and how it was delivered to the prisons. Did you receive any complaints from the users as to the quality and quantity of the food delivered to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of complaints from all the users starting with refugees, our soldiers on the front-lines, and from the administration, that is, the prison staff. Especially difficult was the situation of the people who were delivering this food to the end users. They are the ones who bore the brunt of these complaints. Frequently, they simply stated they would not transport this food to these places, because they cannot explain to the people what the situation was really like. The fighters who would meet us thought that there was more food available and they were always requesting it, but we did not have more food and, had we had more, we would have obviously given it to them. I can only add that the surrounding areas, that is, the villagers lived a little bit better, because they had their own gardens, they had their own livestock. However, the urban population lived in miserable conditions, so from what we had available, we could not provide them with normal rations, so the entire population of this town -- and I believe the situation was similar in other towns -- did suffer physically during the war. I used to weigh 87 kilograms. In this period, I weighed 72 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, it is well known to this Trial Chamber that the detained persons were from the surrounding villages, so my question to you is: when you came to the barracks on your business, could you ever see, and if you could, when could you do that -- did you see members of the families who were coming to visit the inmates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say here I cannot give you the exact date when this was, but I know that this was during the summer. As I was passing through to the warehouses at Celebici, in front of the barracks there was a sizeable number or amount of people -- 30 to 50 persons -- for the most part women and the elderly -- with shopping bags in their hands. I cannot say what was in those bags, whether that was food, cigarettes, or a change of clothes. They would enter and they would drop them off. I cannot say whether they were able to get in touch with the detainees, but I can say with certainty what I have said. As to the Musala prison, I cannot speak to it at all, because I never entered it until the end of the war when the sports hall underwent renovation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me take you back to what your school friend Saran said -- in fact, he did not say anything about his position or the position of other detained persons, so, Mr. Kevric, tell me, during 1992, as a member of the staff, did you find in any other way that persons in the prison were abused or mistreated in any other inhumane way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even though I went to the warehouse in Celebici quite often, I never saw it, and I came during the day and during the night time, depending on the needs of the units that were on the front-lines, but, personally, in the barracks compound, I never saw any kind of abuse.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, do you know whether there were commissions which were supposed to interrogate these detained persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stated yesterday that Mr. Goran Lokas, my school friend from high school, was appointed the president of this commission. I really did not know the other members of the commission, because it is not within my domain, so I could not speak about anyone else from that commission here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally ever hear, either from Goran Lokas or from anyone else, that the detainees were mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When entering the barracks compound, I would enter in a vehicle, I would go straight to the warehouse where the equipment and materiel was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, were you personally ever shown or delivered any kind of report by this commission, or did you ever learn that any kind of report of the commission which investigated the detained persons ever reached the TO staff and a report in which complaints from the prisoners were contained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a member of the staff I never learned about any report on mistreatment of prisoners, or bad conditions in the prison while I was a member of the staff. I simply do not know whether this report ever reached the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, did you ever hear that any person died or was killed in the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I again cannot remember the date, but in Konjic I did hear that Keljo was killed attempting to escape. His name is Keljo and he went to the secondary economic school while I went to the high school, and I really do not know of any other cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, did you ever go to the barracks or to the warehouses with Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never entered the Celebici barracks with Mr. Zejnil Delalic. I never saw him in the Celebici barracks, except on 16 August -- I believe it was 16 August when there was a solemn oath ceremony. On that occasion, Mr. Delalic congratulated all present on having taken the solemn oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kevric, as a member of the staff, do you know whether Zejnil Delalic was a person of superior authority over the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a member of the staff, I did not know that Mr. Zejnil Delalic was the superior person in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have any authority over the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I do not know whether he was a person of superior authority, I cannot say that he was not, but my understanding is, if a person is not a person in superior authority, then he does not have authority over the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether you know that your staff ever gave any authority to Zejnil Delalic with respect to the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, as a member of the staff, the staff never gave such authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, your Honours, no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, Mr. Moran

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I have just a very, very few questions for you, and I think we may be able to get through with this and get you home fairly early. The first thing I would like to ask you about is, was there an incident some time in the middle of July, maybe 12 or 13 July, where some shelling caused a complete break in the supply of bread, where there was no bread available at all for several days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really cannot say now whether that was 12th, 13th or mid July, but I do say that the bakery was shelled and that, during that period, bread could not be baked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And no-one had any bread during that period -- not the soldiers, the refugees, the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bakery was hit, so you could not work there, so people who were there were exposed to shelling -- shelling was taking place in the morning, in the afternoon, sometimes at night, so the production was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Colonel, I am going to ask you a little bit about the camp itself. You are familiar with the layout of both the Celebici barracks and similar facilities that were run by the former JNA, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am completely familiar with the Celebici barracks, because, on 7 January 1993, I became the commander of the logistics base of the 4th Corps, and my base was at the Celebici terminal, so that I do know every single structure there; in other words, I did become familiar with the barracks -- I did become completely acquainted or familiar with the Celebici barracks after 7 January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When the barracks were designed -- and if you do not know, "I do not know" is a fair answer -- do you know how many people it was envisioned would be stationed on the barracks, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already said that the Celebici barracks was envisaged as a terminal for storing fuels. It was not envisaged for housing any personnel, except the personnel which was providing security and administration of the terminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you are talking, what, 10, 20, 30 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have any information regarding the formation that would be deployed there. I only had plans about the structures that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the structures were designed to feed and house a relatively small number of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So, it would have kitchens for a small number of soldiers, toilets for a small number of soldiers, showers -- those kinds of things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was the administration building of the terminal and for the personnel who was providing security for the facility -- there was a small kitchen, there was a small mess hall for about 15 people, and rooms for accommodation of them. There was one toilet and one bathroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Some of the other things that go with having a lot of people around -- both in the Celebici barracks itself and in Konjic -- did you have plenty of, for instance, eating utensils, plates and forks and knives that you could hand out and issue to troops or detainees, or refugees, or was there a shortage of those kinds of things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that yesterday I said that, when we took over the kitchen at the Igman company, we found only about 100 spoons. We did not find any other flatware -- we were able to provide only about 50 plates from the Unevit department store and indeed we had no other utensils. All our soldiers brought utensils from their homes. They even brought with them their blankets, so we were not in a position to provide anything to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That was the next question I was going to ask, Colonel -- blankets -- there was not a warehouse full of blankets some place in Konjic that you could hand out to soldiers and refugees and detainees, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought he had inclusively mentioned things like that when he spoke about soldiers bringing their own blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. When you issued food every day to the army units and the refugees and the prison, did you have a requisition form that was filled out every day so that there would be some kind of a paper trail or was it just done off the lists and you just shipped the food out as best you could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The quartermaster officer in charge and his deputy were involved in this issue. As far as I know, they issued food and they were supposed to issue food in a way that they had to sign off a requisition form, which was available at our warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not on a few occasions there might have been unusual types of things -- food arriving in Konjic, perhaps canned meat might be available on just a few occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I explained yesterday that there were some supplies of sugar in Konjic, so the war presidency swapped some of the supplies of sugar for some canned meat and I believe some canned fish, so we were able to issue soldiers some of that, together with tea so that there would be some variety of food. What I want to say is that, even on that occasion, because we had small quantities of canned meat, especially the 75 gram meat paste cans, they were split three ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And when those were issued to the soldiers, those supplies of meat were also issued to the detainees at the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that the food was prepared in one location and we had a menu for the day and, whatever was on the menu, that was distributed or issued to everyone. There were occasions when the kitchen was also shelled, and it was located in the Igman factory where ammunition was produced, so those facilities were shelled and sometimes it happened that there was shelling, so we had to issue ready-to-eat food to all our end users on certain occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If I were to show you some forms that appear to be requisitions for canned meat or meat pate, could you look at those and tell me if those are the kind of requisition forms that you were used to seeing and the kinds that you used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can look at them and then I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Would the usher help -- I have three different sets of documents -- I have copies for the court and for the Prosecutor, also. (Handed). While the Registrar is preparing the others, those were the kinds of requisitions you used -- you have to say "Yes" or "No", you just cannot nod your head. The court reporter cannot write down a head nod.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we used these forms -- the person who received the goods and the person who issued the goods, and these are the forms that we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What were the numbers of those three exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are marking them for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Just for identification. I am not going to introduce them at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The bill number 60 is Defence Exhibit D23/3; the bill number 44 is Defence Exhibit D24/3; and the last one is Defence Exhibit D25/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Those are the kinds of requisition forms, all three of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gentlemen, your Honours, may I make an additional observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are forms when we are issuing dry food from the supplementary warehouse, but the cooked meals are not included in this form. Bread, which was in the bakery and not in the kitchen, it was also issued on the basis of these forms. That is all I want to say, to make it clear that we were driving from three different points -- cooked food was in one place, bread in another and dry packed food in a third place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. Those three forms that you just looked at would be for the issue of special supplementary food that would not be in the normal menu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were used for the issue of cleaning devices -- sugar and other things that were needed in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So you issued --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Since Mr. Moran is not going to introduce these into evidence, obviously there is no position for me to object. I do want the record to reflect, however, that these documents have not previously been provided to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I personally saw them for the first time late yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose even with that, you could have this morning indicated to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, and my apologies, but one of the reasons I am not tendering them in evidence -- I just wanted them marked and identified -- was to give the Prosecutor time to deal with them if the Prosecutor so chose. Colonel, you said that you issued cleaning supplies and such things to the prison. You issued, for instance, soap for cleaning the facilities and soap for washing your body -- those kinds of things were all issued to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We issued from our warehouse as much as we had, and I cannot assert whether the soap reached the prisoners or not, because that was not within my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine. Your Honour, I will pass the witness, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Because of the skilful, detailed and precise examination of my colleagues, we have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Cross-examination by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, my name is Teresa McHenry and I am going to ask you some questions. If you do not understand the question, please let me know and I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you mentioned earlier that, before testifying, you used a notebook that you had to learn certain dates to refresh your memory about certain dates; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct -- when handing over my duty, and after making my statement, I looked through my documentation and I stand by what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, did you bring your notebook with you to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is a working notebook and I did not bring it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, when you return, will you allow a representative from the Office of the Prosecutor to inspect that notebook?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can have copied the parts that refer to my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, we would ask for any part of your notebook that dealt in any way with a subject that you testified about. Sir, let me ask that you be shown Defence Exhibit 165. This is the document, Sir, that was shown to you yesterday and in which you stated that all the persons on the various lists were part of the TO staff -- part of the TO. (Handed). Sir, I just want to direct your attention to the page, the attachment of the document that has the heading, "Territorial Defence Headquarters Number 05/35-8", dated 28/4/92 -- it is a list of newly enlisted civilians serving in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I explained yesterday that this is a list of persons employed in the municipal staff of Konjic, who were working in the staff before 15 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Maybe I misunderstood you there. What does it mean when it says, "List of newly enlisted civilians serving in the army" -- were these persons that as of 15 April were serving in the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not understand the question. I can comment on all these documents again, if you wish. The first document is a list of persons employed in the municipal staff of Konjic up to 15 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Maybe just to save time, you could explain to me again what this document is, dated 28 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me say, once again, it is a list of persons employed in the municipal staff of Konjic working there before the war, because we had a Territorial Defence in the former system, and they were members of the TO staff. I do not know what is unclear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Well, what is unclear to me is when it says "newly enlisted civilians", does that mean that those people had just joined the TO staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot see this "newly enlisted civilians", where it says that. That is why I am trying to explain the whole document. Maybe we will lose less time in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It is the list that the first name on it is Ivica Azinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is 0/35-8, dated 28 April 1992 -- "newly enlisted civilians". I explained yesterday, because citizens of Serb ethnicity left the staff we needed to fill in the vacancies and these are the people who were enlisted as members of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So let me clarify -- do I understand you to say Ivica Azinovic and Vladislav Andjelic were both members of the TO staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time they were members -- they were members of the TO staff and that is what appears on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, that is all the questions I have for that chart. Sir, am I correct that you had the position of deputy commander of logistics for all of 1992 -- sorry, not for all of 1992, once you got the position in April, you had it for the rest of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said yesterday from 17 April until the end of 1992 I was assistant commander for logistics. Sometimes in the orders it says "for the rear" but it is the same thing, really, for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you indicated that, from your position, you were able to say that the chart prepared by Mr. Cerovac in 1998 was an accurate reflection of the joint command staff in May and June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you able yourself personally to be able to verify and remember all the names that were on Mr. Cerovac's chart, or with respect to some of the positions or some of the names, did you rely on Mr. Cerovac's chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- no, I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown a chart yesterday and it was prepared by someone else, Mr. Midhat Cerovac, in 1998, and you indicated, though, that you could verify that all the names and all the positions on that chart were correct, and my question is: are you yourself able to remember and verify all the names, or with respect to some of them did you have to rely on Mr. Cerovac's chart, because you yourself do not remember or do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why do you not give him the chart?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I can give him the chart. I am now trying to find out whether he knows the information without the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Unless he has a chart before him, how can he say anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If he does not know, he can ask for the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it is a little awkward, the type of question you are asking. Are you suggesting whether he accepts the positions in respect of which people are put down in that chart as a correct one -- I think this is what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes. Let me rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Are you able to say, with respect to each and every name and position that is on the chart, from your own memory, that that is in fact correct -- that the chart is correct with respect to every person and every name, and if you need to look at the chart, certainly, you can?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know very well, because we would sit around a conference table when this organisational chart was made, and the names put in, and then the typist typed it out and it was posted on our board. Now, for me to be able to speak about each individual from number 1 to number 20, it is difficult, but if you give me the document, I will tell you who was where at the time, whether he has left the army now, what duty he is performing, whether somebody has died in the meantime and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am sorry, Sir, are you saying that this organisational chart that you are referring to, that was posted on your board, is this a chart that was made in 1992, or is this the chart that was made in 1998?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which chart are you talking about. Let him have the chart?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is unfair to the witness. Show him the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: With respect to this question, I am only asking because I did not understand his answer. Sir, you just stated that there was a chart, that everyone got around a conference table and put the names in and then it was posted on the board. What chart are you referring to -- a chart that was made in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, if I understand you correctly, you are referring to the chart made by Midhat Cerovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think the witness may be referring to another chart. That is what I am trying to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You started with this particular chart of Mr. Cerovac. This is the chart he is talking about. Let him speak to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness be given the chart, 169. Sir, while it is being given to you, let me just ask a separate question. Was there an organisational chart in 1992, in other words, when you were working in the joint command, was there an organisational chart?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a chart, and on the basis of that chart -- so this chart was made in 1998, but on the basis of the chart compiled in 1992 this chart was probably compiled by Mr. Cerovac. I claim that this chart corresponds to the situation as it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the chart from 1992 still exists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. As I abandoned the municipal TO staff on 7 January 1993, I really could not tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, there is a particular position I am interested in. Who was head of security in the joint command staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The staff -- it is rather difficult to say now, because the headquarters changed places from Musala where the municipal staff of Konjic was located before the war, then the war presidency, then Rudar, then the 3rd March primary school, so it is really difficult for me to say who was in charge of security in the TO staff, whether they were soldiers from the headquarters, from the command, were they jointly organised by the TO and HVO -- I could not tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think maybe my question was not clear. Within the staff of the joint command, was there somebody who was in charge of security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why do you not give him the time frame?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In May and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course there was a person in charge of security -- there had to be somebody in charge of the guards, who may have numbered 5, 10 or 15 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Who was in charge of security in May, as counsel asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not say now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me ask that you look at the chart, which I think has been provided to you. Am I correct that, according to the chart, although you yourself are not able to confirm it, Mr. Goran Lokas was head of the security organ and Mr. Sacir Pajic was his deputy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I did not understand your question. Somebody who is responsible for security and who answers to the security body in the staff, there is a body for security, and this man belongs to the staff, but, for personal security, the security officer may be responsible, so there was a misunderstanding and maybe this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that Mr. Goran Lokas had an accident at the end of May and did not return to the TO -- to the joint command staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether Mr. Lokas had a traffic accident or not, I really do not know, but he did not come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And, after he left -- when he left and did not come back, who was then head of the security organ for the joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you now. Appointments are made by the commander or deputy commander and I really do not know whether it was the officer in the security organ or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know, was there a Mr. Sacir Pajic who had some sort of position in the joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sacir Pajic, as can be seen from this organisational chart, he was in the security organisation and as an officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Let me be clear, I am not now asking you what is on the chart. If it helps you remember, you can look at it, but I am asking you what you yourself know from your own information, and are you able to confirm or are you just not in a position to know whether or not in fact Mr. Pajic had a position in the joint command in May and June of 1992? If you do not know, that is fine, all you have to say is you do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, because that was not within the area of my responsibility or my competence, so I really do not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, am I correct that, with respect to who was in command and what kind of authority they had, you know those persons who were in your area of responsibility or competence, but you do not know about other persons or other positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know with respect to the areas in which I participated, meetings I attended. If decisions were being taken about appointments or some other tasks or combat operations, I know about the meetings I attended, but the security organ did not know what the logistics organ was doing at a given moment -- it was not possible. Everybody could not know what everybody else was doing. Each one of us had his own area of responsibility, so I did not always have to know where an artillery piece would be positioned at a certain point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you should realise that when I am asking these questions they are not critical in any way -- they are just trying to ascertain the facts. So if you can give a simple answer, you should feel free to do so. Unless you feel that the answer is not somehow correct, you really do not need to explain it, because the questions are not meant to be critical. Sir, would you agree with me that the TO commanders in May and June of 1992, Mr. Ramic, Boric and Mr. Ramic again, were appointed by the war presidency, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the war presidency could never appoint a commander of the TO staff. The war presidency could only nominate or propose somebody, but not actually appoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, if Mr. Delalic, Ramic and Boric said otherwise, they would be mistaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question -- could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, let me go on. Sir, did I understand you correctly that the joint command operated in May and June of 1992 and then stopped operating in the end of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct -- it was formed on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, if you need to explain to have it be a fair answer, feel free to do so, but often when I am asking these questions, I am just confirming this so that you know where I am going with my next question and you do not need to repeat something that you have already said yesterday, just in the hope we can move this along a little faster. During the time the joint command was functioning, did the TO retain its own command staff, or was the only command staff operating in Konjic the joint command staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The joint command, as I explained yesterday, was the body in charge of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Did the TO, though, maintain its own separate command staff, just purely within the TO, so that certain persons might have had a position in the TO command staff, but not had a position in the joint command staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I explained yesterday that the commander of HVO units, chief of staff Dinko Zebic and the commander was the commander of the TO units -- the commanding officers belonging to the joint command were appointed by joint signatures, whereas in the units that was not the case -- Commander Zebic appointed his commanding officers in his units with his signature and Mr. Ramic appointed commanding officers of units with his signature, and this applied only to the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So then if I am correct, in May and June of 1992, you were deputy commander of logistics for the joint TO and then you were also deputy commander of logistics for the TO for Mr. Ramic or Mr. Boric, as the case may be; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was not commander but the logistics organ [sic] -- but regarding the actual activities, because the supplies we had were not the same -- the HVO had separate supplies, so we did not receive our resources from the same warehouses. They received theirs from Grude, and they had to have their own man responsible, so there were parallel activities. In those areas in which agreement was reached, the commanders and deputy commanders and chief of staffs would sign, but where there was no agreement, then either Zebic himself or Ramic himself would sign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will break and reassemble at 12 noon. (11.33 a.m.) (A short break) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, Sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Does the witness still have the chart? I may be asking him a question in a minute about the chart (Handed). We were talking, Sir, about what happened at the joint command and the fact that it ended at the end of June. So, in July then, after the joint command ended, the existing command structure of the TO, which continued to exist, then became the only command structure within the TO -- if you do not understand that question, please feel free to tell me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated that, at the end of June, the joint command ceased to function; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you indicated that, on 3 August, Mr. Ramic formally appointed persons such as you to your positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And, am I correct, though, that in July the TO had a command structure which was different than the joint command structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the members of the HVO who were in the joint command were no longer present. That means that we had the TO command structure as it was before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir. When, on 3 August, Mr. Ramic appointed you to that position, you had already been filling that position for a significant period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I explained earlier that I was in the joint command and since there were parallel structures, there was the HVO staff and the TO staff and then they overlapped, so there was personnel in both these separate staffs, but, obviously, there were certain personnel changes -- some people would be moved or transferred to another duty and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What counsel said was not really a question. She was really making a statement that you had been continuously there for all the period -- before the joint command and after the joint command, you were still the same deputy chief of logistics. You held the same position all through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Am I correct that nothing changed on 3 August when you received your formal appointment from Mr. Ramic, at least as far as your position went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing changed in terms of my duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that, whatever the reality of the situation, if you just look at this chart that you talked about, Defence Exhibit 169, the chart would indicate that Mr. Zebic was subordinate to the TO commander. Would you agree with me that if one were only to look at the chart, that is what the chart would reflect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the chart, yes, but if the agreement was not reached, then it would not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, you would agree with me then that the chart does not accurately reflect the reality of the situation as it existed in Konjic at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already stated that there were parallel structures. I explained that if there was agreement, then, yes, but if no agreement was reached, then no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And, indeed, that is why both the TO commander and the HVO commander both signed orders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we saw, they did sign the documents if the agreement had been reached, so, in the case of the Borci operation, the agreement was not reached and Mr. Zebic did not sign it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree with me that there were great difficulties caused by the need to coordinate between the HVO and the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were difficulties with respect to coordination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree with me that there were difficulties caused by the frequent changing of the TO commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is normal that, whenever a commander changes, there are certain difficulties until the commander becomes familiar with all the aspects of his job, especially if such a change happens suddenly. For instance, if the commander is injured or is taken ill and has to suddenly leave his post.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that there were difficulties caused by the problems in communicating with Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were problems in communications with Sarajevo, because the communications did not work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, Sir, that there were many things that were happening in Konjic that were not in accord with traditional military doctrine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you could, would you make your question more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, is it your testimony that, in all respects, such as the operation of the joint command, the structure of the army, the way in which orders were given and received, that this all -- all of it was taking place in accordance with standard military procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my testimony, I have already said that the HVO did not accept the TO staff as the supreme command. Their superior command was the staff in Grude, so the joint command as a joint command did not exist anywhere in our regulation -- it did not provide for a joint command. It should have been part of the TO Konjic. If that is the answer you are looking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your answer is "yes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree with me that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: -- there were many people --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but only on this question that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that there were many people in Konjic who were not even aware of what the standard military procedure was; in other words, there were people in the TO, for instance, who were not always experienced officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because it was -- we had a war, so some people who were appointed to certain positions did not possess all the military knowledge necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would also agree with me that, during this time, there was not always a strict division between civilian and military functions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a division as of 17 April 1992 -- it was clearly defined what the role of the war presidency and the civilian authority was and what was the role of the TO Konjic staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And it is your testimony, Sir, that starting on 17 April, everyone knew exactly what the law provided and everyone followed it exactly -- is that your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which law?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He has referred to the law as of 17 April 1992. I am referring to his answer, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The witness did not refer to a law but to a date, and so he is talking about the work or activities rather than the regulations and in that respect I think it is not a correct question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, what exactly happened on 17 April? You will need to explain it -- was there a new law, was there a new regulation, was there a reorganisation -- I do not need an explanation, but can you clarify what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I already stated this yesterday -- from 17 April on, the commander of the TO staff is not a member of the war presidency as was the case in the previous system in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And on 17 April was the army restructured to change the way that it had been before and the way it was in the future, after 17 April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I explained that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is fine. Sir, is it your testimony, Sir, that on 17 April, in Konjic, that all the reorganisation that was set out in the proclamations from Sarajevo were all carried out in full and understood by everyone in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you expect him to answer that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I believe he has already stated it, so I am asking him to clarify. I am a little surprised, but that is what he said. I am asking if in fact I have understood him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is the question of everybody in the military ought to understand -- not necessarily that everybody did -- it is not a thing one can say and I am sure he is not saying everybody actually did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is His Honour correct that, whether or not everyone should have understood exactly what the reorganisation entailed, that there were some people in the military in fact who did not understand or implement the changes immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I explained yesterday this, but you are now talking about the 1,000 persons and, in the course of mobilisation, I could not have every single recruit medically examined and know exactly who was who, so I cannot tell you this, but the staff was making all the efforts to prevent perhaps efforts of some individuals in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. You would agree with me, Sir, that the war presidency continued to have certain responsibilities to support the military in various ways, in particular, for instance, such as logistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree, it had a duty and obligation, because there was no other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the military supported non-military structures in some ways, such as providing food for companies and refugees in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did this in a single location for all, because we were unable to do it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I am not being critical. If the answer is "yes", all you have to do is say "yes". Sir, you would agree with me that, in addition to serving as the coordinator with the war presidency, Mr. Delalic worked on the problems between the HVO and the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to give a clarification rather than just an answer "yes". As I stated yesterday, he was present at that meeting, so that he could transmit information -- let us say when we talked about logistic problems, he had to transmit the information to the war presidency where there were also Croatian members.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Is it correct that Mr. Delalic also made efforts to smooth out misunderstandings between the HVO and the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He assisted in solving logistical problems, for instance, in a way that he informed the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that previously, in describing Mr. Delalic's role, one of the things you said was that he made efforts to smooth out misunderstandings between the HVO and the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I was clear, but I will repeat it: the HVO was better equipped, they had their own food stocks, and from the supplies that were provided by the war presidency, that is where he mediated, so certain units were already supplied and that is where these coordinations were in relation to the logistical matters. I do not know if you understood me there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I did understand you, but my question had been different. My question had been specifically: you would agree with me that you previously described Mr. Delalic's role as smoothing out misunderstandings between the HVO and the TO -- you would agree that you said that before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did say that, but on those issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is fine. Thank you, Sir. When you were in charge of logistics, did you ever issue written orders to your staff members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Written orders are issued only by the commanders, and are signed by them. As an assistant commander, I did not issue orders -- I can prepare it, but I cannot issue it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I assume you periodically received written orders from your superiors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to ask that you be shown again a document that you were shown yesterday by the Defence from the binder of the expert, V-D/31. I have extra copies and I think it might be easiest if we just have additional copies marked -- I think Ms. Residovic did that mostly yesterday. (Handed). Sir, this is your appointment order dated 3 August, signed by Mr. Ramic, and my question is you will see a number at the very top. It says number 01/277-1, although I think it is a translation error -- I think if you look at the original it says something like "13". Can you tell us what those numbers mean? In particular, is this supposed to be a unique number and thus there would not be other orders with that same number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did look at it and this number means the main staff of the armed forces, when I was appointed, the date is July 1992, and I am being re-appointed because the joint command had split.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I am not sure I understood you answer, if there potentially have been any interpretation issues. Let me say, in the beginning, immediately above the date, where it says "dated 3 August 1992", there is a number and it says number 01/277-13. This is a number that the Konjic municipal staff put on this order; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: My question is: is this a unique number; in other words, is this the only order that is going to have that exact same number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the number of the commander of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, are you saying that every single order from the commander of the staff is going to have that exact same number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should, but sometimes errors occur and sometimes another organ, let us say security and intelligence organ can enter their own number, but the number that should be there should be 01, because each of the organs have their own numbers, but sometimes these things happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Sir, but with respect to the rest of the number, is it the case that there should not be, from the Konjic municipal staff, any other order with the number on it 01/277-13?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: My own copy is different it says "-1".

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am using the interpretation that was supplied to us. I think if you look at the original it looks like it says "13", which I pointed out in the beginning, but we can give it to translation later -- I am just using the document that was provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is your real problem? What are you trying to trace? What is wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I have a question about what these numbers represent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is a question you should be asking from the staff of the commander. You can ask him about the numbers which his staff puts on these documents. How would he know what numbers and how the numbers are? That can only be answered by the staff of the commander which has put the number on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: He stated he was part of the TO command staff and he often received written orders. If he does not know the answer, I think that is fine, but I think it would be a little surprising if he does not know the numbering system of his own command staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If he does not know the answer, I will certainly accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have explained it. An order is signed only by the staff commander. I can prepare the document, but it has to be signed by the commander. If the commander signs it, his number is "01" -- sometimes an error may be made, and the person who compiled the document may put his own number, for example "02", if he is the chief of staff or the assistant commander for logistics. There may be an error, but the "01" stands for the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the numbers that appear after the "01" -- 277-1 or "-13" -- I am not asking you -- all I am asking you is, do you know whether or not these are protocol numbers that were unique to each individual order that was issued by the commander -- do you know the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They should be the protocol numbers. We are still working in the same way -- that is what we do to this day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The protocol numbers are unique to a document, correct, and thus there should not be any other document from the command of Mr. Ramic with the number on it 01/277-13; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there should not be any other document with that number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the document has been written and registered as such, then this number applies to that document only.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You took such a long route to get to merely asking him whether any other letter can have the same number. That is all you needed to ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Sir, this document -- the 3 August document -- the body of it refers to another document dated 11 July from the main staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You would agree with me that Mr. Ramic was head of the TO well before 11 July, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic was from the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you said you were aware of various orders signed by Mr. Delalic as coordinator, many of which concerned logistics. Would you agree with me that not all the orders signed by Mr. Delalic had strictly to do with logistics, or do you simply not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know of the documents which reached me and these had to do only with logistics. I cannot claim anything about anything else if I had not seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But they should not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, can you just tell us what was the relationship between your job and the war presidency, particularly as it relates to logistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relationship between me personally and the war presidency was such that, at the beginning, until Mr. Zejnil Delalic was appointed coordinator, I had to have more frequent contacts. As I realised that this was impossible, and the war presidency also realised that it was impossible for several members of the municipal staff of the TO, of the MUP and the HVO to come, then a coordinator was appointed to mediate between the defence forces and the war presidency regarding supplies of food, equipment, and other means.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you would agree with me that the head of the TO and the head of the HVO and the head of the MUP attended meetings of the war presidency, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: They never attended any meetings of the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I cannot give you an answer without an explanation. The commander of the TO staff was never a member of the presidency; the head of the MUP is; the commander of the HVO staff is not; the coordinator is not. So, I am telling you as it was. Whether sometimes some people were invited, he may have been invited on the 17th when there was a mobilisation -- 17 April -- then all the commanders of the defence forces and the war presidency had to see how to carry out the mobilisation to protect the city, but they were not members of the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, I am sorry, Sir, my question did not ask whether or not they were members of the war presidency; my question asked whether or not, on occasion, they attended meetings of the war presidency, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. The witness has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not the staff commander, I did not attend, I was not present and I did not see, so I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Mr. Delalic a member of the TO, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zejnil Delalic was a coordinator.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Was he also, Sir, a member of the TO, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, you talked a bit about the take-over of Celebici -- the Celebici barracks, when all the weapons were seized. Let me ask you, where were you during the take-over of the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at the farm in Ovcari.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Am I correct that Mr. Delalic and another family member own that farm in Ovcari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zejnil Delalic is not the owner of that farm, but his sister is the owner of that farm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So if Mr. Delalic said he and his sister owned it jointly, he would be mistaken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, the owner of the farm is his sister. She has a house there and I would not go into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Who else was present in the farm in Ovcari while the Celebici barracks were taken over; in other words, I am not asking you right now who participated in the actual military take-over; I am just asking you who was with you at the farm in Ovcari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With me at the farm was Diksa -- his name is Sadik Dzumhur, known as Diksa.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: You would agree with me that Mr. Delalic led the operation to seize the weapons from the Celebici barracks, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would not agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: What was his exact role, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His exact role was to transport the weapons found there by a truck, which he provided, and to transport the weapons to Ovcari.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And can you remember anything about what kind of weapons were captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I received the weapons in Ovcari -- there were automatic weapons, rifles; there were some mines and explosives, cumulative instant rocket-propelled grenades. I am not quite sure whether there was a mortar launcher of 82 millimetres, but I have a precise list of everything that reached the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where is that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The list is in my working notebook. I can copy it and have it sent to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. After the list of the arms was made, the arms were handed over to you at the farm in Ovcari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weapons were handed over at the farm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Who actually, to your knowledge, led this operation to take over the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not know who led the operation. I was informed by the late Velija Niksic that the commander of the security -- his name was Narcis -- I do not know his surname, that he promised him that he would hand over the barracks without any attack, on condition that all soldiers who had served their military service in the JNA are safely transferred to their homes. I know nothing more about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, did you participate in the actions in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Where were you during the actions in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Konjic. Should the need arise for reinforcements and supplies of food and materiel, I was at my work post.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge -- can you confirm that Mr. Delalic also participated in the actions in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know whether Mr. Delalic participated. I said yesterday who was the commander, and I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir. Yesterday you were shown and testified about a document from Sefer Halilovic dated 12 June which concerned the Kralj Tomislav Brigade. It is a Defence document. They showed it yesterday. They did not separately mark it. I have extra copies -- it is V-D/24, but.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Do you want them marked separately?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think it is probably easier to mark it separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is giving it a new number for the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think so. That is what we did yesterday with respect to a number of documents. If the court does not want us to continue that practice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is duplicating the same number for the same document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes.
